scope: 1857 rebellion and its lead-up — annexations under Doctrine of Lapse, the May 1857 outbreak, regional centres (Delhi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Awadh), suppression and aftermath.

events.title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
events.tooltip: Indian Rebellion of 1857 — Meerut outbreak through suppression by 1859
events.summary: Sepoy mutiny at Meerut spread into a 14-month war — Bahadur Shah Zafar declared emperor at Delhi; suppression cost an estimated 800,000 Indian lives.
events.detail: On 10 May 1857 the EIC's Bengal Army sepoys at Meerut mutinied over the greased-cartridge issue (cartridges greased with cow + pig fat for the new Enfield rifle — religiously unacceptable to both Hindu and Muslim sepoys), killed their British officers, and marched on Delhi. The next day they reached Delhi, killed the British residents, and declared the elderly Mughal Bahadur Shah Zafar (then 82) emperor of India — the political act that turned a sepoy mutiny into a full anti-EIC war. The rebellion spread across the Gangetic plain, Awadh, Bundelkhand, and parts of central India: major centres at Delhi (siege June–September 1857), Lucknow (siege July 1857 – March 1858), Kanpur (the Cawnpore massacre under Nana Sahib, July 1857), Jhansi (Lakshmibai's defence June 1858), and Gwalior (Lakshmibai killed June 1858). Nominally suppressed by July 1858 with Delhi's fall and the surrender of major rebel commanders; campaigning continued into 1859. Bahadur Shah was tried, exiled to Rangoon, and died there 1862 — formal end of the Mughal dynasty. The Government of India Act (August 1858) transferred all EIC territory to the Crown. Indian casualties estimated at 800,000 across the campaign and reprisals.

location.name: Delhi (the rebellion's symbolic centre; Meerut was the outbreak)

sources.label: William Dalrymple, The Last Mughal: The Fall of a Dynasty, Delhi 1857 (2006)
C.A. Bayly, Indian Society and the Making of the British Empire (1988), ch. 7

events.title: Letters of Lakshmibai of Jhansi
events.summary: From 1853 protests against Doctrine-of-Lapse annexation through her 1857–58 command, among the few first-person records of a woman rebel leader.
events.detail: Lakshmibai's correspondence survives across two periods. From November 1853, after her husband Maharaja Gangadhar Rao's death, she petitioned the East India Company (and personally Lord Dalhousie) against the annexation of Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse — multiple Persian and Marathi letters citing the adoption of her son Damodar Rao as legitimate heir. Annexation went through in March 1854. The 1857 letters are sparser but extant — communications with Tatya Tope, Nana Saheb, and rebel commanders during the May–June 1858 siege of Jhansi by Sir Hugh Rose, the flight to Kalpi, and the final operations at Gwalior where she was killed on 17 June 1858. Held in the Jhansi state records, the National Archives, and the EIC's London correspondence; her literacy in Persian, Marathi, and Sanskrit, and the survival of her own scribal habits, make these among the few first-person women's records of the 1857 rebellion.

sources.label: Vishnu Bhatt Godse, Maza Pravas (Marathi memoir of an eyewitness; ed. & Eng. trans. Sukhamay Mukhopadhyay, 1974)
Joyce Lebra-Chapman, The Rani of Jhansi: A Study in Female Heroism in India (1986)
